Sedona Red Rocks Day Trip from Phoenix and Scottsdale

Scottsdale Sprinters runs a Sedona day trip from Phoenix or Scottsdale as one vehicle and one chauffeur booked for a 12-hour day: the driver waits at every viewpoint, gallery and trailhead on your list, then brings the group home. The 14-seat Executive Black Sprinter is $145 an hour and that day bills 10 hours: $1,450 before 8% tax, roughly $104 a seat with 14 aboard. Below: how the waiting works, how the hours are counted, which vehicle fits, and how the quote is built. Reservations: (623) 986-6339.

Last updated: September 17, 2026

What is a chauffeured Sedona day trip from Scottsdale?

It is the whole vehicle for a 12-hour window rather than a seat on somebody else's schedule: your group decides who is aboard, which stops are on the list and how long each one lasts. In the 14-seat Executive Black Sprinter at $145 an hour, that day bills 10 hours and comes to $1,450 before tax. You buy a window of time — one vehicle, one chauffeur — agreed in writing before anyone pays, and Scottsdale Sprinters quotes the day rather than a ticket per head. It suits groups a fixed itinerary serves badly: a family pacing the day around grandparents or small children, a company taking clients out of a conference, friends who would rather look out of the window. Per head the arithmetic is plainer than it looks. The Executive Black Sprinter splits $1,450 across 14 seats, about $104 each; the 56-Passenger Motorcoach splits $3,250 across 56, about $58. Those are the current published hourly rates across this day.

How does the day work when the chauffeur waits at every stop?

The vehicle and the driver stay with the group for all 12 hours, parked and waiting while everyone is out. There is no second booking to make, no ride to find afterwards and no meeting point to agree: the 1 vehicle that dropped you off is the one standing there when you come back. The operational block says it plainly: "One pickup address for the whole party and one phone we call. The day is booked as a single hourly charter, so the vehicle and chauffeur stay with you from the first pickup to the last drop-off — the clock does not stop while you are out of the vehicle." That last clause is the product: a stop takes as long as it takes. What waiting buys is mostly the absence of things — no parking to find, no bags to carry between stops, no headcount at a kerb, nobody nominated to stay behind. Coats and shopping stay aboard. And the chauffeur is a resource rather than a fixture: "Ask your chauffeur for anything. Stops, temperature, volume, a photo. Really."

How long is the day, and how are the hours counted?

The tour is published as 12 requested hours, which earn 2 free hours on the standard ladder, so 10 hours are billed. Charters start at a 4-hour minimum, so on a day this long the minimum never binds and the clock runs from the first pickup. The rule that surprises people is the one the block states first: "The day is priced by the hour with a four-hour minimum, and the drive each way is inside the booked window, not on top of it." Getting there and back is part of the day you booked, not a charge bolted onto it, which is why the honest way to read the price is as a day rate. An hourly charter buys time, not mileage, so an extra stop inside the window costs nothing; a stop nobody wrote down was never in the plan. A longer or shorter day than the published one is its own quote.

Which vehicle fits the group on a Sedona day?

Group size decides it, and 8 vehicles are offered for a day tour — proper forward-facing seats, never a limo or a party layout. They run from 8 seats at $1,950 up to 56 seats at $3,250 for the same 12-hour day. Every row prices the identical day: the published hourly rate times 10 billable hours. The per-seat column divides that by seated capacity — friends splitting one fare, never a fare sold per person. Up to 8 travellers the Maybach Shuttle Sprinter answers it; the Executive Black Sprinter and Executive White Sprinter share a rate; past 14 seats the table moves to the mini buses, the Executive Mini Coach (29 Pax) and the 56-Passenger Motorcoach. Cabin space is the second question, and the tour answers it without a bag count: "Pack for a day out rather than a move: layers, water and what you buy along the way. If anyone is being dropped at an airport or a hotel afterwards with full luggage, say so when you book so the fit is confirmed in writing." What does a Sedona day trip from Scottsdale cost?

A 12-hour day in the 14-seat Executive Black Sprinter is $1,450 before 8% tax — $145 an hour across 10 billable hours, because 12 requested hours earn 2 free ones. Split 14 ways that is roughly $104 a seat for the day. Three rules build every number here, and none is specific to Sedona: the day is priced by the hour against the vehicle's published minimum, requested hours above the ladder's rungs earn free hours, and 8% tax is the only addition. Nothing is charged by the mile or per passenger. The Executive Black Sprinter is the least expensive day at $1,450; the 56-Passenger Motorcoach is the least expensive seat at $58 with its 56 seats used. Scottsdale Sprinters takes 50% today by card and the balance is charged 48 hours before pickup. Availability is date-specific, so request a current quote for yours.

What is included on a Sedona day, and what is not?

Included is the vehicle, the chauffeur and every one of the 12 hours, plus bottled water — the only complimentary amenity. Not included is anything the places you stop at charge for. The page says which is which before you book rather than at a counter on the day. In the tour's own words: "Bottled water is on board and it is the only complimentary amenity; meals, entries and anything bought on the way are yours." Entries and meals are what groups most often assume is bundled; what Scottsdale Sprinters sells is the transport and the waiting around it. One house rule matters more on a long day out than on a night in town: "No eating or food inside the vehicle. Drinks are fine; snacks wait for the next stop." In a day built around stops, the next one is never far away.

Is a day trip the right booking, or a one-way ride, a wine day or two days?

This page sells 1 shape only: a chauffeured day that starts and ends at your address with the vehicle waiting in between. The other 3 Sedona bookings are separate pages with their own hours and their own quotes, and each one is linked below rather than half-described here. If nobody needs the vehicle in the middle — a one-way drop-off, or a ride up and a ride back — that is the Phoenix and Scottsdale to Sedona transfer, priced as a transfer rather than as a day. If the day is about tasting rooms, the Verde Valley wine tour is written for it. And if the group wants the red rocks and the South Rim on one trip, that is two days and a separate booking: the Sedona and Grand Canyon combo. Asking one 12-hour day to reach both spoils a good itinerary, because the second comes out of the time at the first.

Where can the day start, and how is it reserved?

Pickup is a street address in any of the 10 metro cities with a published service-area page, not a zone or a depot. Reserving takes 3 things: the date, the number of people and one address, and the answer comes back in writing before a card is charged. The published service areas are Scottsdale, Phoenix, Paradise Valley, Tempe, Mesa, Chandler, Gilbert, Glendale, Cave Creek and San Tan Valley. The tour asks for exactly what the desk needs: "One pickup address for the whole party and one phone we call." One address keeps the group together at the start. Quote online, or call Scottsdale Sprinters on (623) 986-6339 for anything the form cannot price. How it works on the day

Good to know. Bottled water is on board and it is the only complimentary amenity; meals, entries and anything bought on the way are yours.

  • Where we meet you: One pickup address for the whole party and one phone we call. The day is booked as a single hourly charter, so the vehicle and chauffeur stay with you from the first pickup to the last drop-off — the clock does not stop while you are out of the vehicle.
  • Luggage: Pack for a day out rather than a move: layers, water and what you buy along the way. If anyone is being dropped at an airport or a hotel afterwards with full luggage, say so when you book so the fit is confirmed in writing. The Executive Black Sprinter is rated for up to 40 bags.
  • What we can and cannot do: The day is priced by the hour with a four-hour minimum, and the drive each way is inside the booked window, not on top of it. Park, trailhead and site rules are set by the operators there, not by us. Anything the online quote cannot price — an unusual route, a multi-vehicle movement, a vehicle we hold for request only — goes to the reservations desk and comes back as a written quote before any card is charged.
  • What it costs: 12 hours in the Executive Black Sprinter (seats 14): the hour ladder gives you 2 free hours, so you pay for 10: 10 × $145 = $1,450. Add 8% Arizona tax; there is no booking fee and no fuel fee. How the rest settles depends on how you pay: a 50% deposit holds the date and the balance is charged to the card on file 48 hours before pickup; paying in full at checkout leaves nothing else due before your ride; a payment link from the reservations desk is due before the ride.
